- The toolbar’s **Latency** and **Failures** controls change how the mock server behaves. Failures are real 500 responses through the real client, so the error states you see are the ones users would.
- The visual suite pins latency and failures to 0 in the story URL, freezes the page clock at the instant the data was seeded for (so “3 days ago” holds), and waits for `html[data-queries-settled="true"]` on stories tagged `data`. A story that holds a request open on purpose (a loading or pending state) is tagged `busy`.
- Per-story server behaviour comes from `src/app/mocks/overrides.ts`: `hold`, `fail`, `emptyWorkspace`, `malformed`. The database is reset before every story.

```
const meta = {
  title: 'Examples/List page',
  component: ListPage,
  tags: ['!autodocs', 'data'],   // written out: Storybook reads tags statically
  ...mockApiMeta,                // providers, handlers, a fresh database per story
} satisfies Meta<typeof ListPage>;

export const LoadError: Story = { parameters: mswOverrides(fail('get', '/records')) };
export const Loading: Story = { tags: ['busy'], parameters: mswOverrides(hold('get', '/records')) };
export const Linked: Story = { parameters: mockApi({ url: '/records?view=open&q=lease' }) };
```

#### The audit log

- Every admin write emits an audit event where it’s written (the mock server’s member handlers), denied attempts included: the log is a projection of the mutations, not something each page remembers. Actions are `resource.verb` (`member.role_changed`), one per named mutation.
- An event is a snapshot, not a join: it records the actor’s and target’s names as they were. People leave and records are deleted; the log must still say who did what. It is the one place names are copied.
- A date filter is calendar dates in the URL and instants on the wire: `dayRangeToInstants` turns “Sep 1 – Sep 25” into the start of the first day and the start of the day after the last in the reader’s time zone (from `useFormat()`), daylight-saving changes included. Never UTC midnight.
- Record writes don’t emit events yet (their handlers are shared with other work); the seeded history includes them.

#### Adding an entity

- Its schema in `src/app/api/schemas.ts`, and its endpoints (the tenant first) in their own file in `api/`.
- References to other entities as ids, displayed through a ref component or a ref field type: never a copied name.
- Its predicates in `src/app/model`; its projections for lists.
- Its keys (under the partition), queries and named mutations, each mutation with its row in the matrix above, refusing without its capability. A domain added beside the records (the inbox, the admin console) keeps them together in its own module (`src/app/model/inbox.ts`, `admin.ts`), with its contract beside its endpoints in `src/app/api`.
- Its capabilities in `CAPABILITIES`, their roles in `ROLE_CAPABILITIES`, and the same capability on its mock routes.
- Its entry in `entities.ts` (fields, related records, form) and its rows in the route table, each with a guard.
- Mock handlers and seed data (from its own PRNG stream) so its stories and tests run.

<!-- docs/guides/Accessibility.stories.tsx -->

### Accessibility

The target is WCAG 2.2 AA. The system guarantees what can be decided once; product code owns what depends on the page. Both halves are needed.

#### Who owns what

**System guarantees and product responsibilities**

| Area | The system guarantees | Product code owns |
|---|---|---|
| Names and labels | Every control requires its label or accessible name as a prop. Fields wire label, hint and error to the input. | Write labels that make sense out of context. Name icon-only buttons (aria-label plus a Tooltip). |
| Headings and landmarks | AppShell, AuthLayout and FocusedLayout provide the banner and main landmarks (AppShell also navigation and a skip link). PageHeader renders the page’s one h1; PageLayout names its aside. Heading takes a required level. | One h1 per page, then levels in order. Pick the level for the outline; use size for the look. |
| Focus | Visible focus ring on everything. Dialogs, Drawers and menus trap and restore focus; Popovers restore it. Pending buttons and aria-disabled pagination ends keep focus. Scroll containers with sticky bars or headers reserve scroll padding, so focus never lands behind them. | After navigation or a wizard step, move focus to the new h1 (PageHeader’s headingRef) or main. After submit with errors, focus the error summary or the first invalid field. After removing a chip, focus the next one. |
| Colour and contrast | Semantic pairs pass WCAG 2.2 AA in light and dark (tested). Status never relies on colour alone: badges carry text and an icon. | Use the semantic roles as paired. Don’t put text on a colour the pair list doesn’t cover. |
| Announcements | Toasts and Banners announce by tone: danger and warning assertively, info and success politely. Field errors are announced with the field. | Announce the outcome of async work (saved, failed) with a Toast or Banner, not only a visual change. |
| Motion and targets | Durations collapse under reduced motion. Every target is at least 24px or spaced so a 24px circle around it touches nothing else (checked on every story). Nothing is draggable yet; a lint rule makes any drag declare its single-pointer alternative. | Don’t add motion that carries meaning. Keep custom hit areas at least the target-min size. Give every drag a button or menu alternative and name it in data-drag-alternative. |
| Sign-in | Password fields have a show-password toggle. Nothing blocks paste. | Set autoComplete: username, current-password or new-password, one-time-code. No CAPTCHA or other memory or puzzle test without an alternative. |
| Help and repeated input | AppShell’s help slot sits in the same place on every page. | Pass help once, from the app’s shell composition. In a multi-step flow, never ask again for what was already given: show it, prefill it, or let people pick it. |

#### How it’s checked

- Contrast of every semantic pair, light and dark: a unit test on the token source.
- axe (WCAG 2.2 A and AA) on every story in both themes, and on every Docs tab: the visual suite.
- WCAG 2.2 checks axe doesn’t make, on every story: target size, focus not obscured, accessible authentication, consistent help. Plus a lint rule for dragging and unit audits for sign-in and redundant entry.
- Component behaviour (names, states, keyboard): component tests.
- Automated checks find about a third of issues. Before shipping a new flow, use it with the keyboard only and with a screen reader.
- What each check covers, what needs a person and how to run them: [Accessibility conformance](docs/guides/AccessibilityConformance.stories.tsx).

<!-- docs/guides/AccessibilityConformance.stories.tsx -->

### Accessibility conformance

What the build checks against WCAG 2.2 AA, what it can’t, and how to run it. A green build is necessary for a conformance claim, never sufficient.

#### What’s automated

Each check fails the build. Each is proved to fire by a deliberate violation, so a green run can’t mean the check stopped running.

**Automated WCAG checks**

| Criterion | What is checked | Where |
|---|---|---|
| 1.4.3, 1.4.11 Contrast | Every semantic text/background and UI pair, light and dark, computed from the token source. | `npm test` (`tests/unit/contrast.test.ts`) |
| WCAG 2.2 A and AA rules axe can decide | axe on every story in both themes and on every Docs tab. Includes axe’s own target-size rule. | `npm run test:visual` (`tests/visual/stories.spec.ts`) |
| 2.5.8 Target Size (Minimum), AA | Every pointer target, not only the focusable widgets axe measures, is 24×24 CSS px or passes the spacing exception (24px circles), with the inline-text exception. Reports story and selector. | `npm run test:wcag22` |
| 2.4.11 Focus Not Obscured (Minimum), AA | Tabs through every story forward, then backward, and fails when the focused element is entirely covered (by a sticky action bar or table header) or off screen. | `npm run test:wcag22` |
| 2.5.7 Dragging Movements, AA | Lint: an element with `draggable`, an `onDrag…`/`onDrop` handler or a pointer down+move pair must declare `data-drag-alternative`; a file importing a drag-and-drop library must declare one. | `npm run lint` (rule `starter/drag-needs-alternative`) |
| 3.3.8 Accessible Authentication (Minimum), AA | Every story: password fields have `autocomplete` current-password or new-password and a show-password button; no field blocks paste; no CAPTCHA. The sign-in example: `username`, `current-password`, `one-time-code`. | `npm run test:wcag22` and `npm test` (`tests/unit/wcag22.test.tsx`) |
| 3.2.6 Consistent Help, A | Every example page that renders AppShell has its help slot, in the header right before the account menu. | `npm run test:wcag22` |
| 3.3.7 Redundant Entry, A | The setup wizard asks each question once, shows every answer on review, and brings answers back on Edit and Back. | `npm test` (`tests/unit/wcag22.test.tsx`) |

#### How the checks prove themselves

- Story checks: each has a fixture story in `tests/visual/fixtures/`, tagged `check-fixture` and `expect:<check>`, that must fail it. Fixtures are hidden from the gallery (`!dev`) and from screenshots and axe (`no-visual`). A test fails when a check has no fixture.
- Lint rules: a violation in `fixtures/violations/` and a clean control in `fixtures/clean/`, run by `npm run test:rules`.
- Unit audits: each has a negative control, a deliberately bad form or flow the audit must fail.

#### What needs a person

Automated checks find a minority of accessibility problems. Before a release, and before shipping a new flow:

- Keyboard only: complete every core task with no mouse. Focus order follows reading order, focus is always visible and never lands behind anything, and nothing traps it.
- Screen reader: VoiceOver with Safari and NVDA with Firefox or Chrome. Headings, landmarks and names make sense; changes (saved, failed, results updated) are announced.
- Zoom and reflow: 200% text zoom, and a 320 CSS px wide viewport with no horizontal scrolling except for tables (SC 1.4.4, 1.4.10). Text-spacing overrides lose nothing (SC 1.4.12).
- Focus not obscured beyond the gallery: the check runs at one viewport (1024×768) with gallery content. Try narrow widths, where action bars wrap and grow, and real, longer content.
- Target size beyond the gallery: custom hit areas, dense tables and toolbars built in product code, at every breakpoint.
- Dragging: drags wired with `addEventListener` in an effect are invisible to the lint rule. Check that every drag has a working single-pointer alternative, not just a declared one.
- Authentication across channels: codes sent by email or SMS, recovery flows, and any third-party identity step. No step may require remembering, transcribing or solving something without an alternative.
- Consistent help outside AppShell: AuthLayout and FocusedLayout have no help slot yet. If signed-out pages or wizards offer help, keep it in one place across them.
- Redundant entry in every multi-step flow, not only the wizard example: nothing already given is asked for again unless it must be re-entered for security or is no longer valid.
- Windows High Contrast (forced colours) and prefers-contrast: controls, focus and status stay visible.
- Content: link text, error messages and instructions say what to do (see the Content guide).

#### How to run the checks

```
npm run check          # contrast, lint (incl. the drag rule), unit audits, test:rules
npm run test:wcag22    # build the gallery, then the WCAG 2.2 story checks and their fixtures
npm run test:visual    # build the gallery, then screenshots, axe and the WCAG 2.2 checks

# Parallel checkouts: serve each gallery on its own port.
PLAYWRIGHT_PORT=6107 npm run test:wcag22
```

- CI runs every Playwright spec in its visual shards, so the story checks gate a pull request with the screenshots and axe.
- The story checks make one light-theme pass per story (none depends on colour). Most of the time goes to tabbing through each story twice.
- To add a check: write it in `tests/visual/wcag22-checks.ts`, register it in `tests/visual/wcag22.spec.ts`, and add a fixture story that fails it.

#### Claiming conformance

- Publish an accessibility statement: the standard and level, what was tested and how, known limitations with dates to fix them, and a way to report a problem.
- Start from the [Accessibility statement](docs/guides/AccessibilityStatement.stories.tsx) template.
- Procurement often asks for a VPAT (the ACR format): fill it from the same manual audit, criterion by criterion. Don’t mark a criterion Supports on the strength of an automated check alone.

<!-- docs/guides/AccessibilityStatement.stories.tsx -->

### Accessibility statement

A template for the statement a product publishes about its accessibility. Copy it, replace every [bracketed] part, and keep it true: a statement that overclaims is worse than none.

#### Before you publish

- Base the conformance status and known limitations on a manual audit, not on a green build alone.
- List what the build checks and what it can’t: see [Accessibility conformance](docs/guides/AccessibilityConformance.stories.tsx).
- Every known limitation gets an owner and a date. Review the statement at least once a year and after every major release.
- Link it from the app’s help menu and footer, so it sits in the same place on every page.

#### Template

```
# Accessibility statement for [Product]

[Organisation] wants everyone to be able to use [Product], including people who use a
keyboard, a screen reader, magnification, voice control or other assistive technology.

## Conformance status

[Product] is [fully | partially | not] conformant with the Web Content Accessibility
Guidelines (WCAG) 2.2 at level AA. "Partially conformant" means some parts of the content
don't yet meet the standard; they are listed under Known limitations.

## What we do

- Our design system checks colour contrast, target size, focus visibility behind sticky
  content, accessible sign-in and consistent help automatically on every build.
- We test core tasks with a keyboard only and with [screen readers and browsers] before
  each release.
- [Other measures: training, accessibility in acceptance criteria, an owner for this statement.]

## Known limitations

| What | Why it fails | Criterion | Plan and date |
|---|---|---|---|
| [Feature or content] | [What someone can't do] | [e.g. 1.4.10 Reflow] | [Fix by YYYY-MM] |

## Compatibility

[Product] is designed to work with [the two latest versions of Chrome, Edge, Firefox and
Safari] and [VoiceOver on macOS and iOS, NVDA and JAWS on Windows, TalkBack on Android].
It is not designed for [e.g. Internet Explorer].

## How we assessed it

[Self-assessment | an external audit by [auditor]] on [YYYY-MM-DD], covering [scope: pages
and flows]. The report is available on request.

## Feedback and contact

If you find something you can't use, or need content in another format, tell us:

- Email: [accessibility@example.com]
- [Phone or other channel, with hours]

We reply within [N] working days.

## Enforcement

[Where required by law, name the enforcement or complaints body and how to reach it.]

This statement was prepared on [YYYY-MM-DD] and last reviewed on [YYYY-MM-DD].
```

<!-- docs/guides/Content.stories.tsx -->

### Content

Plain, specific and calm. The words are part of the interface: a vague label or a blaming error is a defect like any other.

#### Buttons and links

- Start with a verb and name the thing: “Create record”, “Export CSV”, “Invite user”.
- A confirm button repeats the verb and noun from the dialog title, so it reads correctly on its own.
- Link text says where it goes. Never “click here” or a bare “learn more”.

#### Errors

- What happened, then how to fix it, in one or two short sentences.
- Put it where the problem is: under the field, on the row, or in a page Banner for page-level failures.
- Never blame the user, never show a raw code alone, and never clear what they typed.

#### Casing and words

- Sentence case everywhere: buttons, headings, labels, tabs, menu items.
- One word per concept. If it’s a “workspace”, it’s never also a “team” somewhere else.
- Avoid “please”, “successfully”, “oops” and exclamation marks. Address the user as “you”.
- Labels are always visible. A placeholder is a hint, never the label.

#### Examples

**Write this, not that**

| Where | Write | Not |
|---|---|---|
| Primary button | Create record | Submit, OK, Yes |
| Confirm dialog button | Delete 3 records | Confirm |
| Field error | Enter an amount greater than 0. | Invalid input! |
| Page error | Records didn’t load. Check your connection and try again. | Oops, something went wrong |
| Success toast | Record saved | Your record has been saved successfully! |
| Link | View billing history | Click here |

<!-- docs/guides/Forms.stories.tsx -->

### Forms

Forms are among the most settled patterns in software, and breaking the conventions costs completions. Every control in the system shares one field anatomy, and the create-and-edit example shows the whole flow: validation on blur, an error summary on submit, a pending submit.

#### The field anatomy

TextField, Textarea, Select, RadioGroup, Slider and FileUpload render the same parts in the same order; Checkbox and Switch put the label beside the control.

- **Label**, always visible and required: it is the accessible name. `hideLabel` only where the context says it (a search box in a toolbar).
- **Description** under the control for format hints and consequences (“Shown on invoices”), linked with `aria-describedby`. Never put required information in a placeholder or a Tooltip.
- **Error** under the description, with an icon and text, never colour alone. It sets `aria-invalid` and is read with the field.
- **id**: every control takes one, so an error summary can link to it.
- Mark the rare optional field “(optional)” in its label rather than starring every required one.

#### Which control

**Form controls**

| Control | Choose when | Avoid when |
|---|---|---|
| [TextField](src/components/TextField/TextField.stories.tsx) | Short free text, email, numbers, a password (with its show-password toggle). | More than a line (Textarea), or a value from a known list (Select, RadioGroup). |
| [Textarea](src/components/Textarea/Textarea.stories.tsx) | Free text over a line: a description, a comment. | A single value. |
| [SearchField](src/components/SearchField/SearchField.stories.tsx) | Filtering a list on the page as you type, with a clear button. | A form answer (TextField). |
| [Select](src/components/Select/Select.stories.tsx) | One value from a long or unfamiliar list (six or more). | Two to five options people should compare at a glance (RadioGroup). |
| [Combobox](src/components/Combobox/Combobox.stories.tsx) | One value from a list too long to scan: type to narrow it (an owner, an account). | A short fixed list (Select). |
| [MultiSelect](src/components/MultiSelect/MultiSelect.stories.tsx) | Several values from a longer list, shown as removable chips: event types, tags. | A handful of independent options (Checkboxes). |
| [DatePicker](src/components/DatePicker/DatePicker.stories.tsx) | A calendar date, typed in the reader’s order or picked; ISO in and out. | A moment in time with an hour (a date and a time, stored as an instant). |
| [DateRangePicker](src/components/DatePicker/DateRangePicker.stories.tsx) | A start and an end date in one field and one calendar. | Preset periods (SegmentedControl). |
| [NumberField](src/components/NumberField/NumberField.stories.tsx) | Quantities, amounts (integer minor units with a currency) and percentages, in the reader’s format. | Numbers that aren’t quantities: phone numbers, ids (TextField). |
| [RadioGroup](src/components/RadioGroup/RadioGroup.stories.tsx) | One value from a few options that are all worth reading. | A view switch that applies at once (SegmentedControl). |
| [Checkbox](src/components/Checkbox/Checkbox.stories.tsx) | A yes/no answer, or several independent options, saved with the form. | A setting that takes effect immediately (Switch). |
| [Switch](src/components/Switch/Switch.stories.tsx) | A setting that takes effect the moment it is flipped. | A form answer submitted later (Checkbox). |
| [Slider](src/components/Slider/Slider.stories.tsx) | A position on a scale, or a range, where the exact number matters less: volume, a price filter. | An exact figure (NumberField). |
| [FileUpload](src/components/FileUpload/FileUpload.stories.tsx) | Attaching files, with the limits shown before anyone picks. | Importing rows of data (a dedicated import wizard). |

#### Layout

- One column, in a `Stack`. Short related fields (city and postcode) may share a row in a `Switcher`.
- Group related fields under a heading, or in a `Stack as="fieldset"` with a legend. One `Card` per group on a settings page, each with its own Save.
- The primary action goes last. A long form puts it in a sticky action bar: AppShell’s `footer` slot, or FocusedLayout’s for a wizard. Focus scrolls clear of the bar.

#### When to validate

- On blur, not while someone is still typing into a field for the first time.
- Once a field shows an error, check it on every change, so the error clears the moment it is fixed.
- On submit, check everything. If anything fails, show an error summary above the form, move focus to it, and link each entry to its field. Keep the submit button enabled: a disabled button can’t say what’s missing.
- While submitting, put `loading` on the submit Button: it keeps its label and focus and blocks a second submit.
- Never clear the form on an error. Keep everything the person typed.
- Error copy says what is wrong and how to fix it: “Enter an amount of at least £1”, not “Invalid input”. See Guides/Content.

#### The error summary

A Banner with the problems as links. It isn’t also announced, because focus moving to it already reads it.

```
{problems.length > 0 ? (
  <Banner ref={summaryRef} tabIndex={-1} tone="danger" announce={false}
    title={`There are ${problems.length} problems with this record`}>
    <Stack as="ul" gap="2xs">
      {problems.map((p) => (
        <li key={p.field}><a href={`#${p.id}`} onClick={focusField(p.id)}>{p.message}</a></li>
      ))}
    </Stack>
  </Banner>
) : null}
// After a failed submit: summaryRef.current?.focus()
```

The working version, with every state, is the [create-and-edit example](src/examples/CreateEditFlow.tsx).

<!-- docs/guides/KeyboardPowerUsers.stories.tsx -->

### Keyboard and power users

People who use a product all day stop reaching for the mouse. The system gives them a command palette, one registry for every shortcut, and pickers built for the keyboard, without taking anything away from people who find their way by looking.

#### The test

- An expert can run the core loop without the mouse; a newcomer can still find everything by looking. A shortcut is an accelerator for a visible control, never the only way.
- Every shortcut shows where people will learn it: in the control’s tooltip (`Tooltip shortcut`), its menu item (`MenuItem.shortcut`), its command palette row, and the ? overlay. The same notation everywhere: `mod+k` is ⌘CommandK on a Mac and CtrlK elsewhere.

#### The command palette

⌘K / Ctrl+K from anywhere, or the Search button in the header that shows the keys.

- `CommandPalette` is UI only: a modal dialog with the ARIA combobox pattern (the input keeps focus, ↑ ↓ move, ↵ runs, Esc closes and focus returns), grouped results, forgiving ranking, and the result count announced. The app decides what’s in it.
- The app’s composition (`src/examples/CommandMenu.tsx`) fills it from what already exists, so nobody maintains a list: pages from the route table (every page without params, named by its `title`), records from the list’s own server search, accounts and people from their directories, actions that mirror buttons, and recent items.
- **Only what this person may do.** Every page row asks `can(route.guard)`, the route guard’s own check; every action asks the capability its button asks; records come from the server’s query, so a viewer never finds a draft. A command then does exactly what its button does (the same route, the same session function), so it can’t get past a guard or a mutation’s own refusal. See the [admin](src/examples/CommandMenu.tsx) and [viewer](src/examples/CommandMenu.tsx) palettes for the same query.
- Recent items are kept in the cache partition (`src/app/model/recent.ts`), as ids: they follow the workspace switch, drop with a permission change, clear on sign-out, and show current names.

#### The shortcut registry

One document listener, one list of every active shortcut, one set of rules.

```
useShortcut({
  id: 'inbox.archive',             // stable: conflict reports name it
  keys: 'e',                       // mod+k · shift+? · g i (a sequence) · e
  description: 'Archive',          // verb first: shown in the ? overlay
  scope: 'Inbox',                  // its group in the overlay (default Global)
  handler: archive,                // may change every render
  enabled: targets.length > 0,     // registered, but only fires when it makes sense
});
```

- A shortcut lives as long as the component that registers it: page shortcuts come and go with the page, and the overlay lists what’s active now.
- **Conflicts.** Two active shortcuts with the same keys on this platform (`mod+k` and `ctrl+k` collide on Windows, not on a Mac), or a single key that starts a sequence: the first registration keeps the keys, the second never fires, and the conflict is reported (`console.error`, naming both ids). `findShortcutConflicts` is the same check as a pure function, for a test over a whole app’s shortcuts.
- **Reserved keys are refused** and never prevented: copy, paste, cut, undo, select all, find, address bar, tabs, windows, reload, print, zoom, history (Alt+←/→), Tab, Enter, Space, Escape, arrows, Home/End, Page Up/Down, F-keys, and any Control+Option (VoiceOver) or Control+Alt chord (screen readers). `isReservedShortcut` answers for any keys.
- **Nothing fires** while typing in a field (unless `allowInInputs`, for ⌘ chords only), from inside a dialog (unless `allowInDialogs`), during IME composition, or after another handler took the key.

**Kinds of shortcut**

| Kind | Use it for | Rule |
|---|---|---|
| ⌘ / Ctrl chords (mod+k) | App-wide commands people use from anywhere, including while typing. | Never a chord the browser owns (copy, paste, find, new tab, zoom…): the registry refuses them. |
| Sequences (g then i) | Jumps: two letters, the first a verb ("go"). Many jumps, one prefix. | A single key that starts a sequence conflicts with it (g alone would always fire first). |
| Single keys (j, k, e, ?) | Repeated actions in a queue, where speed matters most. | Can be turned off in the ? overlay (WCAG 2.2 SC 2.1.4); never fire in a text field or a dialog. |
| Keys inside a widget (arrows, Enter, Space, Escape) | The widget’s own model: a listbox, a menu, a grid, a toolbar. | Not for the registry: they are reserved, so page shortcuts can’t steal them. |

#### The app’s shortcuts

**Shortcuts in the example app**

| Keys | Does | Where |
|---|---|---|
| ⌘CommandK | Open or close the command palette | Everywhere, even in a text field (allowInInputs) |
| ? | Show every shortcut active on this page | Everywhere outside a text field |
| GthenH | Go to Home (g r Records, g a Accounts, g p People, g i Inbox, g m Members, g s Settings) | Everywhere; only pages this role may open |
| J | Next item (k: previous) | Lists worked one item at a time: the inbox |
| E | Archive the open item, or the selection | The inbox |
| U | Mark read or unread | The inbox |
| X | Select the open item for bulk triage | The inbox |

- The [inbox](src/examples/InboxPage.tsx) is the reference: j/k move and focus follows, e archives and opens the next, and each key mirrors a toolbar button, a row’s context menu and the bulk toolbar. See [its ? overlay](src/examples/InboxPage.tsx).

#### Keyboard-first components

- `Combobox` and `MultiSelect` (type to narrow, ↑ ↓ ↵), `DatePicker` and `DateRangePicker` (type each segment or use ↑ ↓; the calendar is a grid), `NumberField` (↑ ↓ step, Page Up/Down by ten): React Aria behind the system’s closed API. Dates and numbers follow `LocaleProvider`, the same locale and time zone as `useFormat()`; values stay ISO dates and integer minor units.
- Inside a Dialog their popovers portal into the dialog, and Esc closes only the popover.
- `Toolbar` is one tab stop with arrow keys between its buttons; `ContextMenu` opens with Shift+F10 on the focused row and repeats actions that are visible elsewhere; `InlineEdit` edits one value in place with Enter and Esc; `SplitView`’s divider resizes with the arrow keys.

<!-- docs/guides/Motion.stories.tsx -->

### Motion

Motion gives feedback and shows where something came from. It is short, eased, built from tokens, and it gives way to the reduced-motion preference: nothing in the product depends on seeing it move.

#### Durations

From the token source. The reduced-motion column is what each token becomes under prefers-reduced-motion: reduce.

**Motion durations**

| Token | Value | Reduced motion | Use for |
|---|---|---|---|
| `--motion-fast` | `100ms` | 0ms | Hover and press feedback, colour changes. |
| `--motion-base` | `200ms` | 0ms | Small moves: menus and popovers opening. |
| `--motion-slow` | `300ms` | 0ms | Larger moves: dialogs, drawers, toasts entering. |
| `--motion-spin` | `1000ms` | Unchanged | One revolution of a loading spinner. Not reduced: the spinner is the only progress cue. |
| `--motion-pulse` | `1000ms` | 0ms | One half-cycle of the skeleton pulse. Stops under reduced motion: skeletons don't need to move to read as loading. |

#### Easings

**Easing tokens**

| Token | Use for |
|---|---|
| `--ease-standard` | Movement within the page. |
| `--ease-enter` | Things arriving: decelerates into place. |
| `--ease-exit` | Things leaving: accelerates away. |
| `--ease-linear` | Continuous loops only: spinners, pulses. |

Curves and values are drawn on [Foundations/Elevation and motion](docs/foundations/ElevationMotion.stories.tsx). Things arriving decelerate; things leaving accelerate, and leave a little faster than they came.

#### Writing a transition

Longhands, with a duration and an easing token. The shorthand and literal durations fail lint, and a literal would not collapse under reduced motion.

```
.toggle {
  transition-property: background-color, border-color, color;
  transition-duration: var(--motion-fast);
  transition-timing-function: var(--ease-standard);
}
```

#### What moves, and what never does

- Hover and press feedback, colour changes: `motion.fast`. Menus and popovers opening: `motion.base`. Dialogs, drawers and toasts entering: `motion.slow`.
- Animate `opacity`, `transform` and colours. Never animate layout (width, height, top, margins): it jitters the page and costs a layout on every frame.
- Never animate the focus ring, text people are reading, or a value changing in a table or a Stat: show the new value at once.
- No parallax, no scroll-jacking, nothing that plays on its own for more than five seconds without a way to pause it.
- Never make motion the only signal. The end state must make sense on its own, and async changes are announced with a live region (a Toast, a status).

#### Reduced motion

- The token build writes a `prefers-reduced-motion: reduce` block into tokens.css, so every transition built from tokens collapses to zero without a media query in the component.
- The skeleton pulse stops; the spinner keeps turning, because it is the only sign that work is in progress.
- State still changes instantly: only the movement goes.
- The visual suite runs with reduced motion and animations disabled, so screenshots never catch a frame mid-transition.

<!-- docs/guides/Theming.stories.tsx -->

### Theming and adding a brand

Every alternate look (dark mode, a rebrand, a customer’s colours) is a remap of the semantic token tier. Components read only semantic tokens, so a new theme is a list of values, never a change to a component.

#### How the tiers make it a remap

- **Primitive** tokens are raw values with no meaning: `color.indigo.600`. Nothing in the system reads them directly; a test fails if a stylesheet does.
- **Semantic** tokens say what a value is for: `color.action.primary`, `color.focus`. They alias a primitive, once for light and once for dark.
- **Component** tokens are per-part override hooks (`button.primary.bg`) that alias semantic tokens.
- So a theme changes which primitive each semantic token points at, and everything downstream follows.

#### Dark mode, as built

Each semantic colour holds both values; the scheme picks one.

```
:root { color-scheme: light; }
:root[data-theme="dark"] { color-scheme: dark; }
--color-action-primary: light-dark(var(--color-indigo-600), var(--color-indigo-400));
```

- Components contain no theme rules. Contrast is tested per pair in both schemes, and the gallery captures every story in both.
- Dark depth comes from lighter surfaces, not darker shadows; status and brand colours get their own dark values.

#### What carries the brand today

The semantic colours whose light or dark value comes from the brand ramp. Rebranding means remapping these, and only these.

**Brand-carrying semantic colours**

| Token | Light | Dark |
|---|---|---|
| `color.action.primary` | `color.indigo.600` | `color.indigo.400` |
| `color.action.primary-hover` | `color.indigo.700` | `color.indigo.300` |
| `color.bg.selected` | `color.indigo.50` | `color.indigo.950` |
| `color.fg.link` | `color.indigo.700` | `color.indigo.300` |
| `color.focus` | `color.indigo.600` | `color.indigo.300` |

#### Changing the brand, step by step

For a rebrand of the one product: the house colours change for everyone.

1. Add the new ramp to `tokens/primitive/color.json`, all eleven steps (50 to 950), so light and dark each have room to pick a passing shade.
2. In `tokens/semantic/color.json`, point each brand-carrying token above at the new ramp: the light `$value` and the dark value under `$extensions.starter.modes.dark`.
3. Run `npm run tokens`. It regenerates tokens.css, tokens.ts and the token usage map.
4. Run `npm test`. The contrast test checks every pair in both schemes: link text at 4.5:1 on every surface, the primary fill and the focus ring at 3:1, the label on the primary fill at 4.5:1. A failing pair means a darker (or, in dark mode, lighter) step.
5. Run the visual suite, review the changed screenshots, and regenerate the Linux baselines on the branch.
6. Nothing under src/components, src/primitives or src/layouts changes. If something must, it read a primitive: fix that instead.

#### A second brand beside the first

Not built yet. It arrives with the second brand or tenant, and this is the plan.

- Brand becomes another mode on the semantic tier, beside the scheme: `data-brand` on the root selects a brand’s primitive mapping, `color-scheme` still selects light or dark, and the build writes every brand × scheme combination.
- The contrast test and the visual suite run per brand × scheme, not only for the house brand in light.
- One component set for every brand. Radius, type family and density can be brand tokens; structure can’t. A brand that seems to need different markup is asking for a variant.
- A customer’s colour is untrusted input: check it for contrast when it is saved, and derive or reject the text-on-brand roles rather than shipping a pale primary that fails 3:1.

Until then, the README’s “Deliberately not included yet” table tracks it.

<!-- docs/guides/EscapeHatches.stories.tsx -->

### Escape hatches

Every system component and primitive takes UNSAFE_className and UNSAFE_style. They exist so a deadline never forces a fork, and they are loud on purpose.

#### When an escape hatch is acceptable

- A shipping deadline, and a variant proposal is already open for the look you need.
- Integrating third-party or legacy markup that can’t be changed yet.
- A one-off experiment behind a flag that will be removed or promoted.

Not acceptable: matching a mock that differs from the system, adjusting spacing, or anything a variant or token would cover.

#### The required comment

Consumer code can’t use an `UNSAFE_` prop without an ESLint disable, and the disable needs a description. Write the reason, an owner and a removal condition:

```
{/* eslint-disable-next-line no-restricted-syntax -- matches the partner widget's header height; owner: payments; remove when: Card gets a compact variant */}
<Card UNSAFE_className="partner-card">…</Card>
```

#### Keeping them rare

- Count the disables. A rising count is drift made visible; review it like any other health metric.
- The same override twice is a missing variant. Propose it and remove both overrides when it lands.
- When the removal condition is met, the escape hatch goes in the same pull request as its replacement.

<!-- docs/guides/Contributing.stories.tsx -->

### Contributing and versioning

Anything new starts as a proposal on the decision ladder, lands in one pull request with its stories, docs and tests, and leaves the old way through a deprecation, never a silent removal.

#### 1. Propose

- Walk the [decision ladder](docs/guides/DecisionLadder.stories.tsx) and stop at the first yes: template, variant, component, primitive. Most needs stop at a template or a variant.
- Write a short proposal in the issue or the pull request: the use cases (at least two real ones), the props, an owner, and which existing screens would move to it.
- A second use is the signal to review a local block for promotion; three distinct uses usually confirm the abstraction.
- A repeated escape hatch is a proposal waiting to be written: two screens with the same UNSAFE_ override are asking for a variant.

#### 2. What a pull request must include

- A story for every variant, size and state (open overlays tagged as the Testing guide says), so the visual and axe suites cover it.
- A usage doc in `docs/usage/<Name>.usage.tsx` for every new export: when to use, when not (and what instead), a do, a don’t, and accessibility. The docs test fails without it.
- Tokens and system CSS regenerated with `npm run tokens`, and the token usage map committed.
- `npm run check` green: tokens, types, lint, unit tests, lint-rule fixtures, build, bundle budgets and tree-shaking.
- A new lint rule comes with a violation fixture registered in the rule test.
- A raised bundle budget goes in its own commit, with the old and new limits and what grew.
- The README and the agent rules updated when the parts list or a rule changes.
- In the description: which existing stories render differently on purpose, so their baselines are regenerated and reviewed.

#### 3. Deprecate before removing

- Keep the old name working as an alias of the new one, and mark it in its type so editors strike it through.
- Say what replaces it, and when it goes, in the pull request and the changelog.
- Remove it in a later pull request, after every call site has moved. Grep for it; the build fails on any that remain.

```
/** @deprecated Use Divider. Removed after every screen has moved. */
export const Separator = Divider;
```

A semantic token deprecates the same way: keep the old token as an alias of the new one for the deprecation window.

#### 4. Versioning

Today the system is one folder in one repository, released with the app. Semantic versioning starts when a second app consumes it; the table says how each change will be released then.

**Kinds of change**

| Change | Kind | Today | Once published |
|---|---|---|---|
| A new component, primitive, variant, token or export | Additive | Merge when the checklist is green. | Minor release |
| A bug fix or a visual correction with the same API | Fix | Merge; say which screenshots changed and why. | Patch release |
| Renaming or removing an export, a prop, a variant value or a semantic token | Breaking | Deprecate first (below); remove in a later pull request. | Major release, with a migration note and, for many call sites, a codemod |
| Changing what a token means (not just its value) | Breaking | Add a new token and deprecate the old one; never repurpose a name. | Major release |

Package publishing, a changelog tool and codemods are listed in the README under “Deliberately not included yet”, each with the moment to add it. Until then the pull request history is the changelog.

<!-- docs/guides/Testing.stories.tsx -->

### Testing

The gallery is the test fixture. Every state gets a story, and every story is screenshotted in both themes, checked by axe and by the WCAG 2.2 checks, so a new state is covered the moment it has a story.

#### The suites

**Test suites**

| Suite | Covers | Run |
|---|---|---|
| Unit (Vitest) | Token source and aliases, contrast in light and dark, CSS structure, the token usage map, component behaviour (names, roles, keyboard, focus), the examples, docs coverage. | `npm test` |
| Lint rules | Every ESLint and Stylelint rule fires on its violation fixture, every import boundary is proved, and the clean controls pass. | `npm run test:rules` |
| Visual | A full-page screenshot of every story in light and dark, against Linux baselines. | `npm run test:visual` |
| axe | WCAG 2.2 A and AA rules on every story in both themes, and on every Docs tab. | `npm run test:visual` |
| WCAG 2.2 checks | Target size, focus not obscured, accessible authentication and consistent help on every story; each check proved by a fixture story that must fail it. | `npm run test:wcag22` |
| Budgets | Library JS and CSS size, one component’s cost, and that one import pulls in only what it composes. | `npm run size` (inside `npm run check`) |

```
npm run check                      # tokens, types, lint, unit, rules, build, budgets
npm run build-storybook
PLAYWRIGHT_PORT=6107 npx playwright test --grep "Components/Slider"   # your stories while iterating
PLAYWRIGHT_PORT=6107 npx playwright test                              # everything, once at the end
```

#### A story for every state

- One story per variant, size and state: empty, filled, error, disabled, loading, open. The suites find new stories on their own.
- Stories use fixed data: fixed dates, names and numbers, never `Date.now()` or random values, so screenshots are stable.
- An open modal (Dialog, Drawer, Select, Menu) is tagged `['modal-open', '!autodocs']`. That relaxes only axe’s `aria-hidden-focus`, which can’t see the focus trap. An open non-modal overlay (Popover, HoverCard) takes only `'!autodocs'`.
- Write the tags as a literal array: Storybook reads them statically, and a spread is ignored.
- Behaviour a screenshot can’t show (focus moving, an announcement, a callback) gets a unit test with Testing Library, queried by role and name.

#### Baselines

- Linux baselines are committed and are the source of truth. They come only from the Update visual baselines workflow on the CI image; never edit or delete them by hand.
- Local baselines (darwin, win32) are gitignored. `npm run test:visual:update` rewrites yours, so you can diff your own change before pushing.
- After an intended visual change: run the workflow on your branch, re-run CI, and review every changed image in the pull request. Say in the description which existing stories changed and why.

#### The draft workflow

- Open pull requests as drafts while iterating: they run the check job only, which is fast.
- Mark it ready for review to build the gallery and run the visual, axe and WCAG 2.2 shards. Merge only once that run is green.
- A new push cancels the run it replaces. The gate job, not the shards, is the required check.

#### WCAG checks and rule tests

- What each automated check covers and what still needs a person is on [Accessibility conformance](docs/guides/AccessibilityConformance.stories.tsx).
- A new WCAG check comes with a fixture story (tags `check-fixture`, `expect:<check>`, `!dev`, `no-visual`) that the check must fail.
- A new lint rule comes with a violation fixture in `fixtures/violations/`, registered in the rule test; `npm run test:rules` fails if a rule has none or its fixture stops failing.

<!-- docs/guides/Agents.stories.tsx -->

### Agents

Coding agents read the system from three files at the repo root, generated from the code. Point an agent at llms.txt first: it holds the rules and links to everything else.

#### The three files

- `llms.txt` is the entry point, small enough to read whole at the start of every session (under 16 KB). It follows the llms.txt convention: the name, a summary, the agent rules, then one line per guide, foundation page, component, primitive, layout, utility and golden example, each linking to its file.
- `llms-full.txt` adds every component’s props, variants and states, its usage doc (with the do and don’t code), its stories and tokens, then every guide as Markdown and every semantic token with its light and dark value. Give it to an agent that takes a whole document as context.
- `design-system.manifest.json` holds the same facts as data, for tools and targeted lookups. Its schema, `design-system.manifest.schema.json`, documents every field.

#### How an agent should use them

- Read llms.txt before any UI work and follow its rules. They are the rules below, word for word.
- Building a page: find its archetype under Examples and copy that golden example’s structure. Never copy another screen.
- Before using a component, look it up: its props with their defaults and allowed values, its variants, and “when not to use”, which names what to use instead.
- Need a value: find the semantic token by what it is for (each token carries a description and its light and dark values). Never write a literal.
- Import every `component`, `primitive`, `layout` and `utility` from `src/index.ts`; a `type-only` export with `import type`. No component accepts `className` or `style`: the manifest records that for every one.
- Agent output goes through the same gates as anyone’s: lint, `npm run check` and the gallery.

```
# One component: its props, variants, and what to use instead
jq '.exports[] | select(.name == "Button") | {props: [.props[].name], variants, instead: [.usage.whenNotToUse[].instead]}' design-system.manifest.json

# Which units read a token
jq -r '.exports[] | select(.unit.tokens // [] | index("color.fg.muted")) | .name' design-system.manifest.json

# Text colours, with what each is for
jq -c '.tokens | to_entries[] | select(.key | startswith("color.fg.")) | {token: .key, light: .value.value, dark: .value.modes.dark, use: .value.description}' design-system.manifest.json
```

#### What the manifest holds

- `exports`: every public export of `src/index.ts`, with its kind, source file, status and description. A part (`TableRow`) names the unit it belongs to; a props type names its component.
- For components, primitives and layouts: props (TypeScript type, required, default, description, allowed values), the React DOM attributes they pass through, the closed styling API, variants and states, the usage doc, story ids, the units it composes and every token it reads.
- `tokens`: every semantic and component token with its CSS variable, value, dark value, description and alias chain.
- `guides`, `foundations` and `examples` with a one-line summary each; `rules`; and `commands`, the repo’s scripts.

#### The agent rules

Copied verbatim from CLAUDE.md, between its agent-rules markers. Edit them there.

```
UI rules (design system v0)
- Style only with semantic tokens. No hex, rgb, px, ms or other raw values;
  allowed literals are inherit, currentColor, transparent, none, auto, 0, 1px, 100%.
- Compose system components and layout primitives, imported from src/index.ts.
  Never import radix-ui outside src/components or src/primitives, or
  react-aria-components and @internationalized/* outside src/components.
- Never restyle a system component with className or style. Need a new look?
  Propose a variant. UNSAFE_className / UNSAFE_style are escape hatches that need
  a lint disable with a reason, an owner and a removal condition.
- Before creating a component, walk the decision ladder: template → variant →
  component → primitive. Stop at the first yes.
- Missing token? Add a semantic token in tokens/ (with a dark value for colours),
  run npm run tokens. Never write a literal instead.
- New pages start from PageHeader (the one h1, status, actions) inside the right
  layout: AppShell for signed-in pages (fill its slots; never rebuild the frame),
  AuthLayout for signed-out pages, FocusedLayout for multi-step tasks; PageLayout
  for a page's sub-nav or aside. Copy the matching golden example: list → ListPage,
  record → RecordPage, create/edit → CreateEditFlow, settings → SettingsPage,
  sign-in → SignInPage, wizard → SetupWizard, dashboard → DashboardPage,
  queue/inbox → InboxPage, admin console → AdminConsole, error/404 → ErrorPages.
  Not other screens.
- Links go through Link (or Nav, NavTabs, Breadcrumbs); the app injects its router
  once with LinkProvider. NavTabs for sections that are routes, Tabs for panels in place.
- CSS: inside a declared @layer, BEM-lite classes, logical properties only,
  variants as closed data-* attributes, state via aria/native attributes,
  specificity ≤ 0,3,0, no !important, no ids.
- Every new variant, size or state gets a story. Every new exported component,
  layout or primitive gets a usage doc in docs/usage/<Name>.usage.tsx (when to
  use, when not to, do/don't, accessibility); tests/unit/docs.test.tsx fails
  without one. Lint, npm run check and the gallery (visual + axe + WCAG 2.2 checks) must pass.
- A story that renders an open modal is tagged ['modal-open', '!autodocs'].
- WCAG 2.2 AA is part of the gate: targets ≥ 24px or spaced (size.target-min),
  focus never hidden behind sticky content (scroll containers use
  space.scroll-padding.*), password fields as TextField type="password" with
  autoComplete (username, current-password or new-password, one-time-code),
  never block paste, pass AppShell's help from the shell composition, never
  ask twice in a multi-step flow, and any drag declares data-drag-alternative.
- Never add an eslint-disable or stylelint-disable without a reason after "--".
- Format every number, date, amount and list with useFormat() (LocaleProvider
  sets locale and time zone). Money is integer minor units + currency code.
- AI: render model output with StreamingText (never raw HTML), cite sources
  with Citation + SourcesList, mark unaccepted AI content with AiMarker, and
  never let AI write without ReviewChanges (or an explicit accept) and an Undo.
  The assistant acts only through the person's own can() and named mutations.
- Keyboard shortcuts go through useShortcut (never a bare keydown listener):
  every shortcut mirrors a visible control and shows its keys there (Tooltip
  shortcut, MenuItem.shortcut, Kbd). Reserved keys are refused and conflicts
  reported; single-key shortcuts can be turned off in the ? overlay.
```

#### Keeping them current

Nothing in the three files is written by hand. `npm run manifest` regenerates them, and `npm run check` runs `manifest:check`, which fails when any committed file differs from a fresh build.

- They go stale when an export, a prop, a JSDoc comment, a story, a usage doc, a guide, the token usage map, the agent rules or the README’s Scripts table changes. Run `npm run manifest` and commit the result with the change.
- A description comes from the JSDoc on the export, or else the first “when to use” line of its usage doc. To improve an entry, improve those, never the generated files.

<!-- docs/guides/AiPatterns.stories.tsx -->

### AI patterns

AI in this system is a set of shared parts, not a separate product: streaming answers, inline suggestions, citations, proposed changes with undo, and one assistant that acts only as the signed-in person. Define them once here so every team doesn’t invent its own.

#### Which surface

Put the AI where the work is. The manual path stays beside it, equally visible.

**AI surfaces and their examples**

| Surface | Choose when | Avoid when | Parts | Example |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| Inline suggestion | The next words of a field are predictable and taking them is cheap (Tab). | The result is long enough that accepting it is a decision: use a reviewed block or ReviewChanges. | Suggestion, AiMarker, Kbd | [Create with AI](src/examples/CreateWithAi.tsx) |
| Side panel | Questions about the page the person is on, with the page still in view. | A one-shot transform they’d accept or reject outright: put that action beside the field. | AssistantPanel, ChatThread, Message, Composer, StreamingText, Citation | [Record copilot](src/examples/RecordCopilot.tsx) |
| Proposed changes | The AI would change data: show every change as a diff, applied only after review. | Never skip it for writes, however small. | ReviewChanges, Disclosure or Accordion (steps), AiMarker | [AI bulk changes](src/examples/AiReviewChanges.tsx) |
| Full chat page | Open-ended, multi-turn questions that span the workspace. | Anything tied to one record or one field: keep the AI where the work is. | ChatThread (scroll="page"), Composer in AppShell’s footer, history in PageLayout’s nav | [Assistant chat](src/examples/AssistantChatPage.tsx) |

#### Provenance and citations

- Every claim that matters cites its source. `StreamingText` renders numbered citations through a `Citation` renderer; the `SourcesList` under the answer says where each came from (a record field, an activity entry, a list) and links to it. A citation is a link from the moment it appears: the mock sends sources before tokens.
- Show the work: tool activity (“Read Master cleaning agreement and its activity”, “Found 18 overdue records you can see”) as collapsed `Disclosure`s above the answer, so the person can check what it looked at.
- Mark what the AI wrote with `AiMarker` (text, never colour alone) until a person accepts or edits it. Assistant turns carry it in their header.

#### Consent before acting, and undo after

- The AI suggests; the person decides. Suggestions are ghost text that isn’t the field’s value until Tab or Accept. Changes to data are proposals shown in `ReviewChanges`; nothing is applied until the person accepts changes and chooses Apply.
- Applying goes through the same named mutations as a person’s own edits (`moveRecord`), so it is permission-checked, versioned (a stale proposal gets a 409, reported per change) and patches the cache like any write.
- Keep what was there before. One Undo restores it: the field’s previous text, or every applied record moved back with the version its move returned.
- Stop is always available while an answer arrives, and what arrived stays.

#### What the AI may and may not do

The assistant has no permissions of its own. It is the person, typing faster.

- **Reads** only what the person can see: the mock server filters with the same `canSee` as the list, so a viewer’s assistant never sees drafts, and it reads only its own workspace’s partition; another workspace’s id is not found.
- **Proposes** only what the person could do by hand: a change is proposed only where `can(grant, 'record:move', record)` holds. Without the capability it refuses with the same denial reason a disabled button shows.
- **Asks** the same predicate before sending: `useAssistant` and `useDraftSuggestion` refuse with `can` before any request, controls that start AI actions are disabled with the reason, AI pages have route guards, and every AI route declares its capability on the server.
- **Never** writes on its own, never widens a query past the person’s scope, and never puts another workspace’s data in its context. Requests carry ids and filters, not data: the server reads the data itself, as the person.

```
client    can(grant, 'record:read')  before useAssistant sends        src/app/model/ai.ts
          can(grant, 'record:create') before a draft suggestion       src/app/model/ai.ts
          usePermission(...)          disables Propose / Suggest      src/examples/*
route     guard: record:read | record:create | record:move            src/examples/routes.tsx
server    handle('record:read', ...)  every AI route                  src/app/mocks/ai.ts
          canSee(grant, record)       every record it reads
          can(grant, 'record:move', record)  every change it proposes
apply     moveRecord refuses with can() before sending; the server checks again
```

#### Honest failure and refusals

Each failure has its own words and next step. None of them invents an answer.

**Failure states and what they say**

| State | What it says | Example |
|---|---|---|
| Refused: out of scope | One line: what it can help with instead. Not an error, no Retry. | [Open](src/examples/AssistantChatPage.tsx) |
| Refused: permission | The same denial reason a disabled button shows, and who can change it. | [Open](src/examples/AiReviewChanges.tsx) |
| Rate limited (429) | The server’s message, with when to try again; Retry. | [Open](src/examples/RecordCopilot.tsx) |
| Content filter | The text so far stays; the filter is named; Retry or rephrase. | [Open](src/examples/RecordCopilot.tsx) |
| Connection dropped | The text so far stays; “Nothing was changed”; Retry. | [Open](src/examples/RecordCopilot.tsx) |
| Stopped by the person | The text so far stays, noted as stopped; Retry. | [Open](src/examples/AssistantChatPage.tsx) |

A persistent, quiet disclaimer sits under every composer: “AI can make mistakes. Check important info.”

#### Streaming and accessibility

- `ChatThread` is not a live region (`role="log"` would read every token). Each answer’s `StreamingText` owns one polite status, present from mount: “Generating…”, then each sentence or paragraph once it is complete, then “Stopped” if stopped. It never re-reads the whole answer, and history isn’t announced.
- A suggestion is announced once when it is complete (“Suggestion ready. Press Tab to accept or Escape to dismiss.”), and its text is in the field’s description. The field’s value reads as what was typed.
- The caret and the thinking dots are decorative and hold still under reduced motion (`motion.pulse` is 0). Every AI action has a keyboard path and a single-pointer path (Accept and Dismiss beside Tab and Esc; Widen beside dragging the panel).

#### Model output is untrusted input

- Answers render through the system’s own Markdown renderer, which builds React elements only: no `dangerouslySetInnerHTML`, raw HTML shows as text, links are http(s), mailto or in-app only, images are never loaded (an image URL is a way to leak what’s on screen), and headings become bold text.
- Structured output is validated before it is used: every streamed event is parsed with zod at the boundary, and a malformed one ends the answer as an error rather than rendering half of it. Proposed changes are re-checked by the write path when applied.
- Assume prompt injection: content the AI reads can carry instructions, so it can’t act without the person’s review.

#### Testing AI surfaces

- The mock assistant (`src/app/mocks/ai.ts`) is scripted and seeded: the same question gets the same answer, split into the same tokens. With the gallery’s latency at 0 (the visual suite) an answer completes at once.
- Pin other moments with overrides: `aiHoldAfter(n)` (mid-stream; tag the story `busy`), `aiRateLimited`, `aiContentFiltered`, `aiNetworkDropped`, `aiMalformed`, `aiNoHistory`. Component stories take their text as props, so any moment can be shown without a server.

- `space.gap.lg` `var(--space-gap-lg)`: `24px`. Space between siblings. Layout primitives take these as gap.
- `space.gap.md` `var(--space-gap-md)`: `16px`. Space between siblings. Layout primitives take these as gap.
- `space.gap.sm` `var(--space-gap-sm)`: `12px`. Space between siblings. Layout primitives take these as gap.
- `space.gap.xl` `var(--space-gap-xl)`: `32px`. Space between siblings. Layout primitives take these as gap.
- `space.gap.xs` `var(--space-gap-xs)`: `8px`. Space between siblings. Layout primitives take these as gap.
- `space.inset.2xs` `var(--space-inset-2xs)`: `2px`. Padding inside a box.
- `space.inset.lg` `var(--space-inset-lg)`: `24px`. Padding inside a box.
- `space.inset.md` `var(--space-inset-md)`: `16px`. Padding inside a box.
- `space.inset.sm` `var(--space-inset-sm)`: `8px`. Padding inside a box.
- `space.inset.xl` `var(--space-inset-xl)`: `32px`. Padding inside a box.
- `space.inset.xs` `var(--space-inset-xs)`: `4px`. Padding inside a box.
- `space.scroll-padding.end` `var(--space-scroll-padding-end)`: `80px`. Above a sticky action bar (AppShell, FocusedLayout and Drawer footers). At least the tallest bar.
- `space.scroll-padding.start` `var(--space-scroll-padding-start)`: `48px`. Below a sticky header row (Table). At least the header's height.
- `text.body` `var(--text-body)`: `400 0.875rem/1.5 system-ui, -apple-system, "Segoe UI", Roboto, "Helvetica Neue", Arial, sans-serif`. Default for paragraphs, table cells and form values.
- `text.body-lg` `var(--text-body-lg)`: `400 1rem/1.5 system-ui, -apple-system, "Segoe UI", Roboto, "Helvetica Neue", Arial, sans-serif`. Lead paragraphs and page introductions.
- `text.caption` `var(--text-caption)`: `400 0.75rem/1.375 system-ui, -apple-system, "Segoe UI", Roboto, "Helvetica Neue", Arial, sans-serif`. Helper text, metadata and timestamps.
- `text.code` `var(--text-code)`: `400 0.875rem/1.5 ui-monospace, SFMono-Regular, Menlo, Consolas, monospace`. Inline code and identifiers.
- `text.heading-1` `var(--text-heading-1)`: `700 1.875rem/1.25 system-ui, -apple-system, "Segoe UI", Roboto, "Helvetica Neue", Arial, sans-serif`. The page title. One per page.
- `text.heading-2` `var(--text-heading-2)`: `600 1.5rem/1.25 system-ui, -apple-system, "Segoe UI", Roboto, "Helvetica Neue", Arial, sans-serif`. Page sections and card titles.
- `text.heading-3` `var(--text-heading-3)`: `600 1.25rem/1.375 system-ui, -apple-system, "Segoe UI", Roboto, "Helvetica Neue", Arial, sans-serif`. Subsections.
- `text.heading-4` `var(--text-heading-4)`: `600 1.125rem/1.375 system-ui, -apple-system, "Segoe UI", Roboto, "Helvetica Neue", Arial, sans-serif`. Small groups, card headers.
- `text.label` `var(--text-label)`: `500 0.875rem/1.25 system-ui, -apple-system, "Segoe UI", Roboto, "Helvetica Neue", Arial, sans-serif`. Form labels, buttons, tabs and navigation.
- `z.base` `var(--z-base)`: `0`. Content in normal flow.
- `z.dropdown` `var(--z-dropdown)`: `200`. Panels anchored to a trigger that close on their own: menus, selects, popovers, hover cards.
- `z.modal` `var(--z-modal)`: `400`. Modal dialogs and drawers with their scrim. Everything below is inert while one is open.
- `z.overlay` `var(--z-overlay)`: `300`. Layers over part of the page that aren’t modal: the skip link as it appears, an Imposter’s overlay (inside the Imposter’s own stacking context).
- `z.sticky` `var(--z-sticky)`: `100`. Sticky parts of a scroll container: table header rows, action bars. Above content, below anything that floats.
- `z.toast` `var(--z-toast)`: `500`. Toasts, above modals, so a confirmation sent from inside a dialog stays visible.
- `z.tooltip` `var(--z-tooltip)`: `600`. Tooltips, above everything: they label whatever has focus or the pointer, wherever it is.
